does flame spread faster in microgravity.answer: In microgravity, materials with adequate ventilation may burn more readily compared to normal gravity (1 g) under identical conditions [1]. Specifically, in concurrent-flow comparisons over thin fuel, the microgravity flame reaches a nearly steady-state condition with a convex base, whereas the normal-gravity flame is much longer, sootier, has a concave base, and continues to accelerate over the available fuel length [2]. Additionally, certain fuels that cannot sustain downward (opposed-flow) burning in normal gravity—extinguishing shortly after ignition—will successfully support opposed-flow burning in microgravity [2].

how do smoke particles from overheated m.answer: In microgravity, smoke particles and liquid droplets produced from overheated or pyrolyzing materials tend to be larger than those produced on Earth, with measurements suggesting they are 2 to 8 times larger [1][2][4][5]. This difference occurs because the absence of gravity removes strong buoyancy-induced flows, increasing particle residence times, vapor concentrations, and mixing near the source, which enhances nucleation, condensation, and coagulation processes [2][4][5]. Without gravitational settling and buoyancy, microgravity smoke plumes are spatially symmetric and can contain very large particles exceeding 40 µm, whereas Earth gravity removes large particles through settling and limits terrestrial smoke mode sizes to around 5 µm [2][3]. Furthermore, total particulate mass concentrations can be over five times greater in microgravity [2].

how does smoke differ in microgravity (s.answer: In microgravity, the absence of strong buoyancy-induced flows leads to reduced velocities and mixing, higher vapor concentrations, and increased smoke residence times near the source compared to normal gravity (1-g) [1][2]. These conditions enhance nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, resulting in larger smoke particles and larger droplet sizes for liquid aerosol smokes, along with a corresponding decrease in particle number density for the same mass of smoke [1]. Additionally, low gravity increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector [2].

what was the goal of the acme e-field fl.answer: The goals of the ACME E-FIELD Flames experiment are to establish a fundamental understanding of chemi-ionization and ion-driven convection in microgravity combustion, and to use this understanding to demonstrate the electrical manipulation of sooting behavior and stability limits in the absence of buoyancy [2]. Conducting these tests in microgravity allows for simplifications in analyzing ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling the development of more efficient and less polluting combustion technology for Earth, as well as improving spacecraft fire prevention [1][3].

PSI-69 FLEX: Flame Extinguishment Experiment objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests.
